records.subject: Colton's first independently closed deal
records.context: A small first sale used in a mentoring story.
records.excerpt: So he's brand new, still learning the product line, and he closed his first deal on his own last week. Small account, like four thousand dollars, but he called me practically shaking he was so excited.

records.quote_text: We can't always win on price, steel's steel, but we can win on your stuff shows up when we say it will.

records.quote_text: well, can you put your dad on the phone

records.quote_text: Everybody starts small. I think sometimes owners forget to say that out loud to new people.
records.speaker: Marisol Vance

records.summary: Vance & Kinder won Meridian after a nine-year incumbent missed two rush-order ship dates and shut down a production line.
records.full_story: Meridian had used a competitor for roughly nine years. After that supplier missed two consecutive ship dates on a rush order, Meridian remembered a Vance & Kinder rep from a trade show a year earlier and called because the company had emphasized dependable lead times.
records.setup: Meridian had a long-standing incumbent supplier.
records.tension: The incumbent missed two consecutive rush-order ship dates and caused a production shutdown.
records.action: Meridian contacted Vance & Kinder after remembering its lead-time message from a trade show.
records.lesson: A memorable operational promise can create demand long after the first sales interaction.
records.excerpt: Their old supplier missed two ship dates in a row on a rush order and it cost them a production line shutdown. Their procurement guy called us because he'd met one of our reps at a trade show like a year ago and just remembered we talked a lot about lead times.

records.summary: A longtime customer asked Marisol to put her father on the phone after she took over, then became a top-twenty account and referred two other shops.
records.full_story: After Marisol took over the family business, a customer dating to about 1994 asked to speak to her father. She calmly explained that she had already run operations for three years and handled the order. Two weeks later he acknowledged her expertise. The company remains a top-twenty account and referred two Montana fabrication shops.
records.setup: Marisol had recently taken over her father's company.
records.tension: A longtime customer did not accept that she was now in charge.
records.action: She stayed calm, explained her operating experience, and handled his order.
records.outcome: He recognized her expertise, remained a customer, and sent referrals.
records.lesson: Credibility can be demonstrated through calm competence rather than demanded.
records.excerpt: I didn't get mad, which honestly surprised me. I just said, he retired, but I've been running ops here for three years already, so I promise I know your account better than he does at this point. What do you need? And I just helped him with his order like normal.

records.summary: In a mentoring moment, Marisol encouraged Colton after his first $4,000 close by reminding him that her first sale was even smaller.
records.full_story: Colton, a 24-year-old inside sales rep in his first sales job, closed a roughly $4,000 account by himself and called Marisol shaking with excitement. She told him that everyone starts small and that her first sale after taking over had been smaller than his.
records.setup: Colton was new to sales and still learning the product line.
records.tension: His first independent deal was small, but emotionally significant.
records.action: Marisol contextualized the milestone with her own smaller first sale.
records.outcome: The moment became a concrete example of mentoring new employees.
records.lesson: Leaders should say out loud that everybody starts small.
records.excerpt: I told him I still remember my first sale after I took over, and it was smaller than his. Everybody starts small. I think sometimes owners forget to say that out loud to new people.
